title: Mental Models
head: name
line: Thinking tools investors use to reason, weigh risk and spot their own biases.

items.name: Circle of Competence
items.principle: You do not need to understand everything. You need to understand what matters and recognise what you do not understand.
items.framework: Before investing, ask: Can I explain how this business makes money? Do I understand the industry? Can I identify the key risks? Do I know what would make me wrong?
items.application: This model helps investors avoid investing in unfamiliar industries, following trends blindly, and confusing confidence with competence.

items.name: Margin of Safety
items.principle: Because the future is uncertain, investments should be purchased with a gap between price and estimated value.
items.framework: If a business is worth £100 and it is purchased for £60, the margin of safety is 40 percent.
items.application: Ask what could go wrong, what assumptions must be true, and whether you are paying for perfection.

items.name: First Principles Thinking
items.origin: Aristotle, with a modern application by Elon Musk
items.principle: Avoid accepting assumptions simply because they are common.
items.framework: Instead of asking how everyone else does this, ask what must be true.
items.example: A traditional assumption might be that cars must be expensive to manufacture. First principles thinking asks what the raw materials and actual costs really are.
items.application: Used for understanding industries, finding disruption, and challenging narratives.

items.name: Second-Order Thinking
items.principle: Most people think about what happens next. Great investors think about what happens after that.
items.framework: First order: interest rates are falling. Second order: everyone expects lower rates. Third order: assets may already reflect that optimism.
items.application: Ask what happens next, then ask what happens after that.

items.name: Inversion
items.principle: Avoiding failure is often easier than predicting success.
items.framework: Instead of asking how to succeed, ask how to guarantee failure.
items.example: Common causes of failure include excessive debt, poor management, overpaying, and no competitive advantage. Avoid these first.
items.application: Solving problems backwards surfaces risks that a forward-looking plan can miss.

items.name: Opportunity Cost
items.principle: Every decision has an alternative. Choosing one option means rejecting another.
items.framework: Before investing, ask: if I had cash today, would I buy this investment over every other alternative available right now?
items.application: Prevents holding mediocre investments, emotional attachment, and poor capital allocation.

items.name: Incentives
items.principle: People respond to incentives.
items.framework: Analyse management incentives, executive compensation, customer behaviour, and industry incentives.
items.application: Ask what behaviour a given system encourages.

items.name: Base Rates
items.principle: The past provides useful probability estimates.
items.framework: Instead of asking whether something could happen, ask how often it actually happens.
items.example: A company claims it will become the market leader. The base rate is that most companies fail to achieve dominance.
items.application: Grounds ambitious claims in historical frequency rather than possibility alone.

items.name: Bayesian Thinking
items.principle: Good investors change their minds when facts change.
items.framework: Start with an initial belief, such as a 60 percent probability. As new evidence appears, increase or decrease that probability, and base the next decision on the updated information.
items.application: Avoids confirmation bias and ego attachment to an original view.

items.name: Probabilistic Thinking
items.principle: The future cannot be known with certainty.
items.framework: Instead of saying a stock will rise, think in probabilities: for example, a 60 percent chance of a positive outcome, a 30 percent chance of a neutral one, and a 10 percent chance of a negative one.
items.application: Replaces false certainty with a distribution of possible outcomes.

items.name: Systems Thinking
items.principle: Individual events are often caused by wider systems.
items.framework: Analyse inputs, processes, outputs, and feedback loops.
items.example: Company success can be traced as a chain: product leads to customers, which leads to revenue, then cash flow, then reinvestment, then growth.
items.application: Helps investors see a business as an interconnected system rather than a single number.

items.name: Compounding
items.principle: Time amplifies repeated good decisions.
items.framework: Capital multiplied by return multiplied by time equals wealth creation.
items.application: Applies to money, knowledge, skills, and relationships, not just capital.

items.name: Skin in the Game
items.principle: Incentives improve when decision makers share the outcome of their decisions.
items.framework: People should experience the consequences of their own decisions.
items.application: Analyse insider ownership, management incentives, and alignment between management and shareholders.

items.name: Lindy Effect
items.principle: Durability is evidence. The longer something survives, the longer it may continue to survive.
items.framework: Businesses with long histories, strong brands, and repeat customers may possess resilience that newer businesses have not yet proven.
items.application: Treats survival over time as data, not just sentiment.

items.name: Regression To The Mean
items.principle: Extreme outcomes often move back toward the average over time.
items.framework: Exceptional periods are difficult to maintain forever.
items.application: Ask whether a period of unusually strong performance is sustainable.

items.name: Narrative vs Reality
items.principle: Humans are attracted to compelling stories.
items.framework: A narrative might claim a company will change the world. Reality is found instead in revenue, margins, cash flow, and competitive advantage.
items.application: Separates the story being told about a company from the evidence underneath it.

items.name: Confirmation Bias
items.principle: Investors naturally protect their existing opinions.
items.framework: The tendency to seek information that supports existing beliefs.
items.example: Before investing, write down the answer to: why might I be wrong?
items.application: Forces an explicit search for disconfirming evidence rather than supporting evidence alone.

items.name: Availability Bias
items.principle: Recent or easily remembered events feel more probable than they actually are.
items.framework: Investors may fear another 2008 crisis or dot-com crash, or feel unusual excitement about a recent winning stock, simply because those events are memorable.
items.application: Separate what is memorable from what is actually probable.

items.name: The Margin of Error
items.principle: Good decisions allow room for mistakes.
items.framework: Build conservative assumptions, strong balance sheets, and sensible valuations.
items.application: Accepts uncertainty rather than assuming a forecast will be exactly right.

items.name: The Investor Checklist
items.principle: Checklists improve consistency and reduce emotional decisions.
items.framework: Before buying: understand the business, know the competitive advantage, assess management, understand valuation, identify risks, define why you could be wrong, and decide position size.
items.application: Replaces memory and mood with a repeatable process.

items.name: Survivorship Bias
items.principle: The visible successes are often not representative of the full population.
items.framework: It is easy to look at the best investors who became billionaires while ignoring the thousands who attempted similar strategies and failed.
items.application: Ask what examples are missing, whether only winners are being studied, and what failed companies once looked promising.

items.name: Loss Aversion
items.principle: People feel losses more strongly than equivalent gains.
items.framework: The pain of losing £1,000 is usually greater than the pleasure of gaining £1,000.
items.application: Explains panic selling, holding losing positions, and fear during crashes. Ask whether a rational decision is being avoided because of emotional discomfort.

items.name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
items.principle: Past costs cannot be recovered. Only future outcomes matter.
items.framework: An investor might think they cannot sell because they already lost 50 percent. A better question is whether they would buy this company today with fresh cash.
items.application: Redirects decisions toward the future rather than the past.

items.name: Endowment Effect
items.principle: Ownership creates emotional attachment.
items.framework: People overvalue things simply because they own them, for example favouring a stock because they own it rather than owning it because the evidence supports it.
items.application: Separates genuine conviction from attachment created purely by ownership.

items.name: Dunning-Kruger Effect
items.principle: Limited knowledge can create excessive confidence.
items.framework: Beginners often underestimate the complexity of what they are attempting.
items.application: Early investors may overtrade, believe they can predict markets, and ignore risk.

items.name: Expected Value
items.principle: Good decisions can produce bad outcomes, and bad decisions can produce good outcomes. Judge the process, not any single result.
items.framework: Expected value is probability multiplied by outcome.
items.example: A 70 percent chance of a £100 gain and a 30 percent chance of a £50 loss gives an expected value of £55.
items.application: Evaluates decisions by their probability-weighted outcomes rather than by hindsight.

items.name: Decision Trees
items.principle: Complex decisions become clearer when broken into branches.
items.framework: An investment might succeed if revenue grows, margins improve, and competition remains limited, and fail if debt increases or demand declines.
items.application: Maps possible outcomes before acting rather than reacting to a single scenario.

items.name: Power Laws
items.principle: A small number of outcomes create a disproportionate amount of results.
items.framework: A small number of companies create most market wealth, and a few investments typically drive most of a portfolio's performance.
items.application: Explains why portfolio returns are often concentrated in a handful of holdings.

items.name: Pareto Principle (80/20 Rule)
items.principle: A minority of causes create the majority of effects.
items.framework: Focus on the 20 percent of information that drives 80 percent of the decision, such as competitive advantage, management quality, and cash generation.
items.application: Directs research time toward what actually matters most.

items.name: Network Effects
items.principle: A product becomes more valuable as more people use it.
items.framework: Social platforms, payment networks, and marketplaces are common examples.
items.application: Strong network effects can create defensibility, pricing power, and long-term advantage.

items.name: Switching Costs
items.principle: High switching costs create customer retention.
items.framework: Enterprise software, banking relationships, and business systems are common sources of switching costs.
items.application: Look for businesses where customers are unlikely to leave.

items.name: Economies of Scale
items.principle: Size can create competitive advantages as businesses grow.
items.framework: Large companies may negotiate better prices, spread fixed costs, and improve margins as they grow.
items.application: Explains why cost advantages often widen as a business gets bigger.

items.name: Optionality
items.principle: The ability to choose later is valuable.
items.framework: Maintaining choices creates value even before those choices are used.
items.application: Strong companies often have multiple growth opportunities, strong balance sheets, and strategic flexibility.

items.name: Anti-Fragility
items.principle: Some systems become stronger through stress and uncertainty.
items.framework: Businesses that adapt quickly, gain market share during crises, and learn from competition can be considered anti-fragile.
items.application: Looks for businesses that improve under pressure rather than merely surviving it.

items.name: Barbell Strategy
items.principle: Combining extreme safety with a small amount of selective risk.
items.framework: A portfolio can pair a large, safe foundation with a small number of high-upside opportunities.
items.application: Balances protection with opportunity, rather than spreading risk evenly across the middle.

items.name: Game Theory
items.principle: Investment decisions do not happen in isolation. They involve the responses of other participants.
items.framework: Analyse competitor behaviour, industry dynamics, and management incentives.
items.application: Helps investors anticipate how competitors and other market participants are likely to respond.

items.name: Prisoner's Dilemma
items.principle: Individual incentives can conflict with collective outcomes.
items.framework: Companies competing through destructive price wars are a common business example.
items.application: Helps investors understand industry-wide behaviour, not just one company in isolation.

items.name: Reflexivity
items.principle: Markets are not purely objective. Investor beliefs affect prices, behaviour, and company decisions.
items.framework: Rising prices can attract more buyers, which pushes prices higher still, feeding back into the fundamentals themselves.
items.application: Reminds investors that a rising or falling price can shape reality, not just reflect it.

items.name: Second-Level Effects
items.principle: Considering unintended consequences beyond the first, obvious effect.
items.framework: Lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper as a first effect, but a second effect is that asset prices may become inflated.
items.application: Extends thinking past the immediate, most visible outcome.

items.name: Informed Contrarianism
items.principle: Being different is not enough. An investor must be different and correct.
items.framework: Ask why the market is wrong, supported by evidence, rather than simply taking the opposite position.
items.application: Distinguishes genuine, evidence-based contrarian views from contrarianism for its own sake.

items.name: Bayesian Updating
items.principle: Strong investors are not attached to being right. They are attached to getting closer to the truth.
items.framework: An initial belief that a company has a strong competitive advantage can be updated by new evidence such as margin decline, customer losses, or a new competitor, leading to an updated belief that the advantage may be weakening.
items.application: Avoids confirmation bias, ego attachment, and holding outdated beliefs.

items.name: Anchoring
items.principle: The first number or idea received can influence future judgement.
items.framework: A bad anchor sounds like: this stock used to trade higher, or I bought it at a certain price so it must return there. A better anchor is business value and future cash flows.
items.application: Redirects judgement away from a remembered price and toward the underlying business.

items.name: Recency Bias
items.principle: Recent experiences feel more predictive of the future than they actually are.
items.framework: After a crash, investors say markets are dangerous. After a bull market, investors say markets always rise.
items.application: Ask whether a view is reacting to history or only to the last few months.

items.name: Complexity vs Simplicity
items.principle: Complexity can create the illusion of intelligence.
items.framework: A great investment thesis should answer what the company does, why it will succeed, and why it is undervalued. If the answer requires excessive complexity, understanding may be weak.
items.application: The best solutions are often simpler than expected.

items.name: Goodhart's Law
items.principle: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.
items.framework: A company rewarded for increasing sales may see sales increase while profitability declines.
items.application: Look beyond revenue growth, user numbers, and reported metrics to understand whether they represent real value.

items.name: Campbell's Law
items.principle: The more pressure placed on a metric, the more likely it is to become manipulated.
items.framework: Possible manipulation includes adjusted earnings, aggressive accounting, and short-term incentives.
items.application: Ask whether a company is improving the business or improving the numbers.

items.name: Checklist Thinking
items.principle: Experts use systems because memory and judgement fail under pressure.
items.framework: Before investing: understand the business model, identify competitive advantages, assess industry dynamics, check revenue quality, profitability, balance sheet strength, and cash generation, confirm management incentives and capital allocation ability, apply reasonable valuation expectations and a margin of safety, and ask why you could be wrong and what would change your mind.
items.application: Uses structured processes to reduce mistakes rather than relying on memory alone.

items.name: The Map Is Not The Territory
items.principle: All frameworks simplify reality.
items.framework: A valuation model is not the business. A forecast is not the future. A financial statement is not the entire company.
items.application: A model or explanation is not reality itself, and should be held loosely rather than mistaken for the thing it describes.

items.name: TEI Investor Decision Framework
items.origin: A combination of Graham, Buffett, Munger, Marks, and behavioural finance
items.principle: A complete operating system for investment decisions, bringing together the models before it.
items.framework: Step 1, Understand: what am I buying, covering business model, customers, industry, and competitive advantage. Step 2, Assess Quality: is this a great business, analysing management, economics, growth, and durability. Step 3, Analyse Value: what is it worth, considering cash flows, assumptions, expectations, and price. Step 4, Assess Risk: what could go wrong, identifying business, financial, valuation, and behavioural risks. Step 5, Make A Decision: is this the best use of capital, comparing alternatives, opportunity cost, and portfolio position. Step 6, Monitor: what would change my mind, defining success conditions, failure conditions, and review points.
items.application: Provides a repeatable six-step process to apply to every investment decision, from understanding the business through to ongoing monitoring.
